extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in philosophical and psychological theories of humor
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic survey of major philosophical and psychological theories about laughter and humor, their historical lineage, strengths, weaknesses, and examples. Useful for evaluating explanatory accounts of what makes things funny and the ethical/social dimensions of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor’s Bad Reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical and normative objections to laughter and humor from Plato, Aristotle, Stoics, early Christian thinkers, medieval monastic rules, and Puritans—treating laughter as morally suspect, destructive of self-control, linked to idleness, lust, anger, or as malicious scorn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains common lines of criticism (e.g., Plato: laughter overrides rational self-control; Philebus: ridicule as vice; Biblical examples linking laughter to hostility). Gives historical examples and institutional responses (monastic bans, legal/social sanctions, Puritan rejection of comedies). Use when evaluating claims that humor is morally or socially harmful; consider whether laughter at a target is loss of self-mastery, malicious scorn, or socially corrosive. Shows anti-pattern: treating all laughter as morally equivalent without distinguishing type (scornful vs witty vs benign).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Superiority Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim (from Plato, Hobbes, Descartes, and later proponents) that laughter expresses feelings of superiority over others or over a former state of oneself—'sudden glory' or delight in another’s perceived inferiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives classical sources (Hobbes’ 'sudden glory', Descartes' derision), and modern proponents (e.g., Roger Scruton). Includes counterexamples and limits discussed by Hutcheson and others: laughter without comparison (wordplay), laughing at one’s present self, laughing at displays of skill, and experimental results (Deckers weight task) that challenge necessity/sufficiency of superiority. Use as an explanatory criterion but test for counterexamples; anti-pattern: over-generalizing superiority to explain all laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Relief Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter functions to release pent-up nervous or psychic energy (hydraulic model) — associated historically with Shaftesbury, Spencer, Dewey, and Freud’s broader ideas about discharge of nervous/psychic energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes versions: Shaftesbury’s release of 'animal spirits', Spencer’s discharge of nervous energy as muscular motion without object, Dewey’s laughter as relaxation of strain. Notes contemporary criticisms: the hydraulic physiology is outdated; many funny things don't evoke pre-existing emotion to be released (e.g., wordplay), and empirical objections to Freud/Spencer claims. Use when considering physiological/therapeutic interpretations of laughter; anti-pattern: assuming every laugh corresponds to venting previously built-up affect or repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freud’s three laughter situations (der Witz, the comic, humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud’s taxonomy within a relief-style account: der Witz (jokes/witty remarks) releases energy used to repress feelings (libido/hostility); the comic releases energy normally used for thinking (mimetic representation); humor releases affective energy by suppressing distressing affects 'in statu nascendi'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples (sexual/hostile jokes, clownish clumsiness, Mark Twain story) and explanatory mechanisms Freud proposes. The entry highlights substantive criticisms: questionable psychoanalytic claims about repression as joke source, problematic 'mimetic representation' account, and empirical evidence that joke preferences do not align with repression patterns. Use cautiously as a historical/theoretical model; treat Freud’s specific energetic bookkeeping as contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Incongruity Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises from perceiving something incongruous—violations of mental patterns or expectations (set-up/punch). Prominent in Beattie, Kant, Schopenhauer, Kierkegaard, and now dominant in philosophy and psychology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains core meaning: violation of expectations or mental patterns. Gives classical authorities: Aristotle’s advice (create expectation then violate it), Cicero on disappointed expectation, Kant’s requirement that expectation be 'transformed into nothing' (not into its opposite), Schopenhauer’s concept-perception mismatch, Kierkegaard’s 'contradiction'. Discusses how this maps onto modern joke-writing (set-up vs punch), wordplay, and cognitive accounts. Use as central evaluative criterion for many jokes; note variation among theorists over what counts as incongruity and necessary additional conditions (e.g., harmlessness, resolution). Anti-pattern: treating any surprise as incongruity without specification of cognitive mismatch or resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up and Punch (joke structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical, structural criterion: the set-up creates an expectation; the punch (line) violates that expectation, producing the incongruity that may lead to laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout historical discussion as an example of incongruity in practice. Examples: wordplay, sudden reinterpretation of context, silent-film stunts. Helpful for analyzing joke construction and for producing humor (crafting an expectation and a violating twist). Anti-pattern: overreliance on surprise without adequate semantic or conceptual linkage for the punch to register as humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schopenhauer / Concept–Perception Mismatch
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific form of incongruity: humor results when there's a sudden perception of mismatch between abstract concepts (generalizations) and particular sense perceptions of objects or situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer’s account locates the incongruity between our abstract classifications and concrete perceptions (e.g., concept 'dog' vs particular Chihuahua vs St. Bernard). Explains why being laughed at is offensive (reveals mismatch between conception and reality) and why we enjoy the victory of perception over thought. Use this when analyzing jokes that hinge on category slips, misapplication of general concepts, or conceptual over-generalization. Anti-pattern: conflating all expectation-violations with concept–perception mismatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as Play; Laughter as Play Signal
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory that humor evolved from mock-aggressive play (seen in apes), and that understanding humor as play helps answer philosophical objections and reveals benefits (social, cognitive) shared with play and philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains evolutionary/ethological background (rough-and-tumble play, play signals), and argues that viewing humor as play mitigates charges of malice and self-control loss by framing many instances as sanctioned, non-serious interaction. Use when evaluating social functions of humor (bonding, practice, signaling) and when distinguishing playful vs hostile laughter. Includes benefits and normative defenses of humor. Anti-pattern: treating all laughter as play when clear malicious or harmful mockery is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy (nature, distinctions, and social function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical account of comedy as a form of humor distinct from other sorts of laughter—concerns about comic vs tragic, the harmlessness criterion, the comic vision of life, and ethical/aesthetic dimensions of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draws on Aristotle’s Poetics, Kierkegaard, Hazlitt, and modern commentators: the ridiculous is a mistake or unseemliness that is not painful or destructive; comic apprehension sees contradictions but in a painless way. Discusses comedy’s role in culture, its moral evaluation (when comedy is abusive vs insightful), and the 'comic vision' as philosophically significant. Use when assessing extended comic works, genres, or the ethical limits of comedic practice. Anti-pattern: equating brief jokes with comic art without attending to scale, narrative, or moral impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and Moral Criteria for Evaluating Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative considerations about when humor is morally permissible or blameworthy: concerns about malice, ridicule, demeaning targets, racism/sexism, and whether a sense of humor can be a virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes philosophical debate (Plato, Kant, modern discussions) about malicious laughter versus benign wit, the offensiveness of being laughed at, Puritan/monastic condemnations, and contemporary work on racist/sexist jokes and moral limits. Points to factors relevant for evaluation: intent of laugher, target vulnerability, social context, whether laughter expresses scorn or playful signaling, and potential harms. Use as a checklist when judging the ethical acceptability of humor; anti-pattern: judging humor solely by its formal features (incongruity/surprise) without considering moral context.
